description: Solo participant working on the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge.
summary:
Lunar Constraint Navigator is an interactive web application that explores how assumptions about sunlight and Earth visibility can change comparisons of locations near the lunar south pole.

Using NASA/JPL Horizons ephemeris data, we analyze five lunar locations over December 2026. The application compares hourly Sun-center and Earth-center elevations, counts hours that satisfy user-defined elevation thresholds, and examines continuous 48-hour windows. An interactive assumption explorer shows how the relative ranking of locations changes when those thresholds vary.

For example, at the Mons Kocher feature center, the number of hours meeting both conditions falls from 16 out of 744 to zero when the assumed Sun elevation threshold increases from 0° to 1°, while the Earth threshold remains at 0°.

The project addresses the challenge by making the sensitivity of lunar site comparisons transparent and explorable. It is a preliminary geometric screening and educational tool, not a landing-site recommendation or a model of terrain obstruction, power availability, or landing safety.
details:
Lunar Constraint Navigator is an interactive scientific web application for exploring how assumptions affect comparisons of locations near the lunar south pole.

What the project does

The application compares five lunar locations: the IAU feature centers of Mons Mouton, Mons Malapert, and Mons Kocher, and the historical landing locations of IM-1 Odysseus and IM-2 Athena. It uses NASA/JPL Horizons ephemeris data to examine the geometric elevations of the Sun and Earth during December 2026.

Users can compare hourly conditions, adjust minimum Sun and Earth elevation thresholds, and investigate continuous 48-hour windows. The Assumption Explorer evaluates 2,601 threshold combinations, allowing users to see how rankings and eligibility counts change across different assumptions. The Time-Window Explorer helps users examine when conditions occur rather than relying only on monthly totals.

Why it matters

Lunar south-pole exploration involves difficult trade-offs because the Sun and Earth can remain close to the local horizon. Small changes in screening assumptions may produce large differences in apparent suitability.

For example, the Mons Kocher feature center satisfies both baseline geometric conditions for 16 of 744 hourly samples. Increasing the assumed Sun elevation threshold from 0° to 1°, while keeping the Earth threshold at 0°, reduces that count to zero.

The application also reveals close comparisons, such as the 408-versus-409-hour baseline result for Mons Mouton and IM-2 Athena. Rather than presenting a single ranking as definitive, it encourages users to investigate how robust that ranking is.

How it was developed

The application was built using React, TypeScript, Vite, and Recharts, with Python-based data processing and validation. NASA/JPL Horizons data provide the underlying ephemeris calculations. The interface presents comparison tables, interactive visualizations, threshold sensitivity analysis, and time-window exploration.

The project includes reproducible calculation methods, explicit assumptions, source references, and documented limitations. Automated tests and browser-based checks were used to verify the implementation.

Creativity and intended impact

The central innovation is treating assumptions as variables to explore, rather than hiding them behind a fixed site ranking. The project turns a potentially misleading single-number comparison into an interactive investigation of sensitivity, uncertainty, and interpretation.

It is intended to support scientific education, early-stage geometric screening, and clearer discussion of lunar exploration trade-offs.

Scientific limitations

This is not a landing-site recommendation or a landing-safety assessment. The model uses geometric Sun-center and Earth-center elevations and does not account for local terrain horizons, physical illumination, communications link performance, power systems, or engineering constraints. IAU feature centers are not proposed landing coordinates, and historical landing locations are included for comparison rather than future mission selection.
